sets.title: The Four-Day Working Week
text: A growing number of companies around the world are experimenting with a four-day week, hoping to improve staff {{1}} without reducing output. Early trials suggest that, {{2}}, employees often get just as much work done in four days as they used to in five.

One of the main concerns before the trials began was that a shorter week would make the workplace less {{3}}, but most managers found the opposite was true. Teams became better at {{4}} their time, cutting out long meetings and unnecessary emails.

Not everyone is {{5}}, though: some workers in client-facing roles say a four-day week is simply {{6}} in their industry, since customers expect {{7}} support throughout the week. Even so, supporters argue that with careful planning, almost any job can adapt {{8}}.

sets.title: Why Some People Fear New Technology
text: Throughout history, {{1}} inventions have often been met with suspicion rather than excitement. When fingerprint scanners first appeared on phones, some people genuinely believed companies could steal a person's {{2}}.

Psychologists suggest that this kind of {{3}} often comes from a fear of the unknown rather than any {{4}} evidence that the technology is dangerous. In fact, most fears about new inventions turn out to be {{5}} once people become familiar with them.

Even so, experts warn against {{6}} dismissing every concern as irrational, since some worries about privacy and safety are perfectly {{7}}. The challenge for society is the careful {{8}} of new technology, rather than rejecting or accepting it without question.

sets.title: The Lost Art of Getting Lost
text: Before smartphones, travellers often had no choice but to rely on paper maps and a certain amount of {{1}}. Many older travellers say they miss the {{2}} of discovering a hidden café purely by accident.

GPS apps have made travel far more {{3}}, since it is now almost {{4}} to get seriously lost in a city. However, some psychologists argue that this gradual increase in convenience has {{5}} reduced our sense of direction.

A small number of travel companies now offer {{6}} tours that deliberately avoid maps and itineraries, encouraging guests to wander {{7}} and see what they find. Supporters say the {{8}} of a little uncertainty is part of what makes travel memorable.

sets.title: The Science of a Good Night's Sleep
text: Doctors increasingly describe sleep as a {{1}} part of good health, not an optional extra. Yet a surprising number of adults experience regular sleep {{2}} without even realising it.

Experts recommend going to bed at a {{3}} time each night, since an irregular schedule can confuse the body's internal clock. People who sleep well also tend to report feeling more {{4}} and better able to concentrate the next day.

Poor sleep has also been linked to {{5}} decision-making and a {{6}} immune system, making people more likely to catch common illnesses. {{7}}, researchers say that even small improvements, such as avoiding screens before bed, can make a noticeable difference. For most people, better sleep begins with {{8}}, not expensive gadgets or supplements.
